title: Kafka Topics & Partitions: The Field Notes
summary: A dense, practical handbook on how Kafka topics and partitions actually work — from log mechanics and ordering guarantees to keys, partitioners, replication factor, ISR, and the durability trade-offs behind acks and min.insync.replicas.

chapters.title: 1. Topics, Partitions & the Log
points: Topic = named logical stream of records; a category, not a queue with a single tail.
Partition = the real unit of storage and parallelism; a topic is just a set of N partitions.
Each partition is an append-only, immutable, ordered commit log — writes only ever go to the end.
Offset = monotonically increasing 64-bit integer, unique WITHIN a partition, assigned by the leader on append.
Offsets are NOT unique across a topic: partition 0 and partition 1 both have an offset 42.
Record anatomy: key (nullable), value (nullable), timestamp, headers, partition, offset.
Reads are non-destructive: consuming does not delete the record; N consumer groups read the same bytes independently.
Consumer position is just a stored integer (offset) per (group, topic, partition) in the __consumer_offsets topic.
Partitions map to directories on the broker: /kafka-logs/orders-3/ holds segment files for topic `orders`, partition 3.
Segments: each partition splits into segment files (default 1 GB or 7 days), named by base offset — 00000000000000012345.log.
Index files (.index by offset, .timeindex by timestamp) let a broker seek to a byte position without scanning the log.
Only the active (newest) segment is written; older segments are immutable and eligible for retention/compaction.
Retention is time- or size-based (retention.ms, retention.bytes) and deletes whole segments, never individual records.
Log end offset (LEO) = next offset to be written; high watermark (HW) = highest offset replicated to all ISR.
Consumers can only read up to the high watermark — uncommitted records are invisible, so a lost leader cannot un-deliver data.

chapters.title: 2. Ordering Guarantees: What Kafka Really Promises
points: The core promise: total order WITHIN a partition. Nothing more.
There is NO global ordering across partitions of a topic — ever, at any config.
Two records written to different partitions have no defined relative order, even if written microseconds apart.
Corollary: order is preserved only for records that share a partition, which in practice means share a key.
A single consumer reading one partition sees records in exactly the offset order they were appended.
Ordering survives replication: followers replicate the leader's log byte-for-byte in order.
Ordering is per-partition per-producer-session for a plain producer; retries can reorder without idempotence (see ch. 6).
Design rule: choose the key so that everything that must be ordered together shares it (e.g. key = accountId for a ledger).
Partition count changes break historical ordering: adding partitions re-maps keys, so old and new records for one key can sit in different partitions.
Ordering ≠ delivery timing: consumer lag differs per partition, so partition 5 may be minutes behind partition 2.
Multi-topic ordering is undefined — a `payments` event and an `orders` event have no cross-topic sequence.
Timestamps do not restore order: log-append time is monotonic per partition, create time is client-supplied and can go backwards.
Consumer-side parallelism (thread pool per record) destroys ordering even when Kafka preserved it — use a key-hash executor.
Comparison row: RabbitMQ per-queue FIFO vs Kafka per-partition FIFO — Kafka trades global order for horizontal scale.

chapters.title: 3. Keys & Partitioners: How a Record Picks Its Home
points: The producer, not the broker, decides the partition — assignment happens client-side before the network call.
Default rule with a key: partition = murmur2(keyBytes) % numPartitions (Kafka's own murmur2, not Java hashCode).
Same key + same partition count = same partition, forever, across producers, languages, and restarts.
Null key, modern clients (2.4+): sticky partitioner — fill one partition's batch, then switch. Better batching, fewer requests.
Null key, old clients (<2.4): plain round-robin per record, which produced many tiny batches.
Explicit partition in ProducerRecord overrides everything — the escape hatch, and the easiest way to create skew.
Code: `new ProducerRecord<>("orders", order.customerId(), payload)` — key is the second arg, not a header.
Custom partitioner: implement `Partitioner.partition(topic, key, keyBytes, value, valueBytes, cluster)`, set `partitioner.class`.
Use a custom partitioner for tenant isolation, geo-affinity, or pinning a hot key to a dedicated partition.
Key cardinality must exceed partition count by a wide margin, or partitions sit empty: 3 keys over 12 partitions uses 3.
Hot key = one key with a huge share of traffic — it pins to one partition and that partition becomes the bottleneck.
Hot key fixes: composite key (`userId#bucket`), key salting, or a two-stage aggregate; each costs you strict per-user order.
Keys also drive log compaction: compaction retains the latest value per key, so a null key makes a record uncompactable.
Tombstone = record with a key and a null VALUE — signals delete-this-key to a compacted topic.
Gotcha: key serializer must be stable. Changing from String to Avro key encoding re-partitions every key silently.

chapters.title: 4. Partition Count: Parallelism, Sizing & Regret
points: Partition count is the parallelism ceiling: at most one consumer per partition within a consumer group.
20 partitions + 30 consumers in one group = 10 idle consumers, permanently.
Adding consumers past the partition count buys zero throughput — add partitions or split the work downstream.
Multiple groups scale independently: each group gets its own full assignment of all partitions.
Rough sizing: partitions = max(target_throughput / per_partition_producer_rate, target / per_partition_consumer_rate).
Per-partition throughput is commonly 10 MB/s+, but consumer processing cost usually binds first.
Partitions can only be INCREASED, never decreased — `kafka-topics.sh --alter --partitions 24` is one-way.
Increasing partitions re-maps the hash space: existing keys move, breaking per-key order and compaction history.
Never increase partitions on a compacted topic in place — the same key can then exist in two partitions.
Per-partition cost on brokers: open file handles, memory for index buffers, and one replication fetch stream per follower.
Cluster-wide cost: leader election and metadata propagation time scale with total partition count — a controller failover concern.
KRaft removes the old ZooKeeper metadata bottleneck; clusters handle far more partitions, but per-broker file/memory cost stays.
Producer memory: `batch.size` is allocated per partition per producer, so 1000 partitions × 32 KB = 32 MB of buffer pressure.
Practical guidance: start with a partition count you can live with for a year; over-provisioning modestly beats resharding.
Trade-off row: few partitions = tighter ordering, cheaper metadata, weak parallelism. Many = high parallelism, more rebalance/latency cost.

chapters.title: 5. Replication Factor, Leaders & Followers
points: Replication factor (RF) = number of copies of each partition, placed on distinct brokers.
Every partition has exactly one leader and RF−1 followers, assigned per-partition, not per-topic.
All produces and (by default) all consumes go through the leader; followers are pure replicas.
Followers replicate by issuing normal fetch requests to the leader — the same protocol consumers use.
Leadership is spread across brokers so a 3-broker cluster with 6 partitions gives each broker 2 leaderships.
RF=1 means zero redundancy: a single broker loss loses the data permanently. Only for scratch/dev topics.
RF=3 is the production default: tolerates one broker down while still allowing writes with min.insync.replicas=2.
Fault tolerance = RF − 1 broker failures survivable for availability; durability limits are tighter (see acks/ISR).
RF is set at creation (`--replication-factor 3`) and changed later only via `kafka-reassign-partitions.sh` with a JSON plan.
Reassignment copies whole partitions over the network — throttle it (`--throttle`) or it starves live traffic.
Rack awareness (`broker.rack`) spreads replicas across racks/AZs so one AZ loss does not take all copies.
Preferred leader = first replica in the assignment list; auto.leader.rebalance.enable restores it after recovery to avoid leader skew.
Storage math: RF multiplies disk. 1 TB of topic data at RF=3 is 3 TB of cluster disk plus retention headroom.
Follower fetching (KIP-392) lets consumers read from a nearby replica to cut cross-AZ transfer cost, trading a little staleness.
Unclean leader election (`unclean.leader.election.enable=true`) lets an out-of-sync replica take over — availability bought with silent data loss.

chapters.title: 6. In-Sync Replicas (ISR) & the Durability Contract
points: ISR = the set of replicas (leader included) fully caught up with the leader's log.
"Caught up" means the follower fetched within `replica.lag.time.max.ms` (default 30s) — time-based, not message-count-based.
Old `replica.lag.max.messages` was removed because a legitimate traffic burst falsely evicted healthy followers.
A lagging follower is removed from ISR; when it catches up to the leader's LEO it is added back.
High watermark = min LEO across the ISR; only records at or below the HW are committed and visible to consumers.
`acks=0`: fire and forget, no ack, records lost on any failure. Highest throughput, no durability.
`acks=1`: leader writes to its log and acks. Lost if the leader dies before followers replicate.
`acks=all` (`acks=-1`): leader acks only after every ISR member has replicated the record.
`acks=all` alone is NOT enough — if ISR shrinks to just the leader, "all" means one replica.
`min.insync.replicas` (broker/topic config) is the guard: if ISR size < it, produces with acks=all fail with NotEnoughReplicasException.
The production triple: RF=3, min.insync.replicas=2, acks=all — survives one broker loss, still refuses to write below 2 copies.
RF=3 with min.insync.replicas=3 has no failure headroom: one broker down and the topic stops accepting writes.
Availability/durability trade-off: raising min.insync.replicas increases durability and decreases write availability. Always.
Idempotent producer (`enable.idempotence=true`, default in 3.0+) adds producer id + sequence number so retries do not duplicate or reorder.
Idempotence requires `max.in.flight.requests.per.connection` ≤ 5; without idempotence, in-flight > 1 plus retries can reorder a partition.

chapters.title: 7. Consumer Groups, Assignment & Rebalancing
points: Consumer group = set of consumers sharing a group.id; the group collectively owns every partition exactly once.
Group coordinator (a broker) tracks membership; the group leader (a consumer) computes the assignment.
Rebalance triggers: member joins, member leaves, member times out, or topic metadata changes (new partitions).
Range assignor: per-topic contiguous ranges — simple, but skews when partition count is not divisible by consumer count.
RoundRobin assignor: balances across all subscribed topics, but reshuffles almost everything on each rebalance.
Sticky / CooperativeSticky assignor: preserves prior assignments where possible, moving the minimum set of partitions.
Eager rebalancing (old): every consumer revokes everything, stop-the-world pause across the group.
Cooperative incremental rebalancing (KIP-429): only the partitions that actually move are revoked; the rest keep processing.
Static membership (`group.instance.id`) skips a rebalance entirely on a short restart within session.timeout.ms.
`session.timeout.ms` covers heartbeat liveness; `max.poll.interval.ms` covers slow processing — a long poll gap kicks the consumer out.
Classic bug: slow per-record processing exceeds max.poll.interval.ms, consumer is evicted mid-batch, work is reprocessed, lag grows further.
Manual assign() (no group) pins partitions explicitly: no rebalance, no automatic failover — you own the assignment.
Offset commit semantics: auto-commit (at-most/at-least-once depending on failure point) vs commitSync after processing (at-least-once).
Exactly-once needs the transactional producer (`transactional.id`) plus consumer `isolation.level=read_committed`.
Consumer lag per partition (end offset − committed offset) is THE health metric — watch max lag, not average.

chapters.title: 8. Retention, Compaction & Partition Data Lifecycle
points: `cleanup.policy=delete` (default): whole segments dropped once older than retention.ms or the partition exceeds retention.bytes.
`cleanup.policy=compact`: retain at least the latest value for every key, forever — the log becomes a changelog/table.
`cleanup.policy=compact,delete`: compact, and still age out very old data — common for Streams changelogs with bounded history.
Compaction runs per partition and never touches the active segment, so the newest records are always uncompacted.
Because compaction is per-partition and keyed, changing partition count splits a key's history across partitions and corrupts the table view.
Tombstone (key, null value) marks a delete; retained for `delete.retention.ms` (default 24h) so consumers can observe it.
`min.cleanable.dirty.ratio` (default 0.5) controls how dirty a log must be before the cleaner touches it.
retention.bytes is PER PARTITION, not per topic — a 10 GB setting on 12 partitions permits 120 GB per replica set copy.
Common mistake: sizing disk with retention.bytes as a topic total, then filling the disk 12× over.
Time retention keys off the record timestamp, so a backfill with old create-times can be deleted immediately on arrival.
Segment roll settings (segment.bytes, segment.ms) determine deletion granularity — huge segments delay reclaiming space.
Tiered storage (KIP-405) moves cold segments to object storage so a partition's retention exceeds local disk.
Comparison: delete-policy topic = event stream (facts over time); compacted topic = latest-state table (materializable).
Reprocessing depends on retention: seekToBeginning() only replays what retention still holds.

chapters.title: 9. Failure Modes, Gotchas & Anti-Patterns
points: Skewed partitions from a hot key: one partition at 90% of traffic while eleven idle. Check per-partition byte rate, not topic rate.
Null keys where order mattered: sticky partitioning scattered a user's events across partitions and broke sequencing.
Increasing partitions on a live keyed topic: same key now hashes elsewhere, so ordering and compaction history both break.
acks=all with min.insync.replicas=1: durability theatre — a single-replica ISR still satisfies "all".
unclean.leader.election.enable=true: cluster stays available by promoting a stale replica and silently truncating committed records.
Retries without idempotence and in-flight > 1: a retried batch lands after a later batch, reordering the partition.
auto.offset.reset=latest on a new group: silently skips the entire existing backlog on first start.
auto.offset.reset=earliest after retention expiry: reprocesses everything still on disk, flooding downstream systems.
Consumer thread pool per record: Kafka's ordering guarantee held, the application discarded it. Shard by key-hash instead.
Too many partitions: slow controller failover, heavy producer memory, and long rebalances that look like a broker outage.
Too few partitions: consumers cannot scale out, and the fix (adding partitions) is the destructive operation above.
Rebalance storms from max.poll.interval.ms too low relative to processing time — each eviction causes more lag, causing more evictions.
Assuming cross-partition order in a join or aggregation: correct only if both sides are co-partitioned on the same key with the same partition count.
Assuming a consumer read is durable-forever: it reads up to the high watermark, but retention may delete it before a replay.
Monitoring gaps to close: UnderReplicatedPartitions, OfflinePartitionsCount, IsrShrinksPerSec, max consumer lag, per-partition byte rate.

chapters.title: 10. Cheat Sheet & Decision Rules
points: Ordering: guaranteed per partition. Want ordering for an entity? Give it a stable key.
Parallelism: bounded by partition count per group. Want more consumers? More partitions first.
Partition formula (keyed): murmur2(key) % numPartitions. Unkeyed: sticky batching, partition undefined.
Durability default: RF=3, min.insync.replicas=2, acks=all, enable.idempotence=true.
Availability tuning: min.insync.replicas=1 for uptime-first pipelines; accept possible loss on leader failure.
Never enable unclean leader election unless availability strictly outranks correctness, and document that choice.
Sizing rule of thumb: target throughput ÷ per-partition consumer throughput, then round up for headroom.
Key design rule: cardinality ≫ partition count, and the entity that needs order must be the key.
Compacted topic rule: pick the partition count once, never change it, always key every record.
retention.bytes is per partition — multiply by partitions × RF to get real disk.
acks table: 0 = no wait / can lose everything; 1 = leader only / loses on leader failure; all = full ISR / bounded by min.insync.replicas.
ISR table: in ISR = counted for acks=all and the high watermark; out of ISR = ignored, cannot be a clean leader.
Debug order: partition skew → consumer lag per partition → ISR shrink events → rebalance frequency → disk/retention.
Useful commands: `kafka-topics.sh --describe` (leaders, replicas, ISR), `kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe` (lag), `kafka-configs.sh --describe` (topic overrides).
The one-line summary: Kafka gives ordered, replicated, per-partition logs — the key chooses the partition, the partition count caps parallelism, and ISR plus acks decides what "written" really means.
